paragraphs: For me, this affair began when I read a notice in the obituary section of the Gentleman’s Magazine from an early year of the nineteenth century:

On February 26th, at his home in the Cathedral Close of Barchester, the Venerable John Benwell Haynes, D.D., aged 57, Archdeacon of Sowerbridge and Rector of Pickhill and Candley. He attended —— College, Cambridge, where his talent and diligence won him the respect of his seniors. When he took his first degree at the usual time, he ranked highly among those awarded first-class honours in mathematics. These academic honours soon secured him a Fellowship of his College. He was ordained in 1783 and shortly afterwards appointed to the permanent curacy of Ranxton-sub-Ashe by his friend and patron, the late, truly venerable Bishop of Lichfield.… His rapid promotions, first to a prebendary’s post and then to the office of Precentor in Barchester Cathedral, eloquently testify to the respect he commanded and his outstanding qualifications. He became archdeacon after the sudden death of Archdeacon Pulteney in 1810. His sermons always upheld the principles of the religion and Church he did so much to honour. To an unusual degree, and without the least trace of religious excitement, they combined a scholar’s refinement with a Christian’s grace. Free of bitter sectarian feeling and inspired by the spirit of the truest charity, they will remain long in his listeners’ memories. [A further omission here.] His writings include an able defence of government by bishops. Although the writer of this tribute has often read it, it provides yet another example of the lack of generosity and enterprise all too common among the publishers of our generation. His published works are, in fact, limited to a lively and elegant translation of the Argonautica of Valerius Flaccus, a volume of Discourses upon the Several Events in the Life of Joshua delivered in his Cathedral, and a number of the formal addresses he gave to the clergy during his various inspections of the Archdeaconry. These are distinguished by etc., etc. Those who knew him will not readily forget his courtesy and hospitality. His devotion to the venerable, awe-inspiring building, beneath whose ancient vault he attended so punctually, might be called that of a son. This was especially true of his interest in the music of its services. It formed a strong and delightful contrast to the polite indifference shown by too many of our cathedral dignitaries today.
After telling us that Dr Haynes died unmarried, the final paragraph says:

One might have expected so peaceful and benevolent a life to end at a ripe old age, with an equally gradual and peaceful death. But how impossible it is to understand the workings of Providence! The quiet retirement in which the honoured evening of Dr Haynes’s life was mellowing towards its close was destined to be disturbed—indeed, shattered—by a tragedy as appalling as it was unexpected. On the morning of February 26th—
But perhaps I had better hold back the rest of that account until I have told the circumstances that led to it. As far as these can now be discovered, I have learnt them from another source.

I had read the obituary I have been quoting entirely by chance, along with a great many others from the same period. It had given me a little cause for speculation. I thought that, if I ever had the chance to examine local records of that time, I would try to remember Dr Haynes. Beyond that, I made no effort to investigate his case.

Very recently, I was cataloguing the manuscripts in his college library. I had reached the end of the numbered volumes on the shelves, and asked the librarian whether there were any more books he thought I should include in my description. ‘I don’t think so,’ he said, ‘but we had better look at the manuscript section and make sure. Have you time to do that now?’ I had. We went to the library and checked off the manuscripts. At the end of our inspection, we came to a shelf I had not seen before. It mostly held sermons, bundles of incomplete papers, college exercises, Cyrus, an epic poem in several cantos written by a country clergyman in his spare time, mathematical papers by a deceased professor, and other material of a kind I know only too well. I made brief notes on these. Finally, we pulled out and dusted a tin box. Its badly faded label read: ‘Papers of the Ven. Archdeacon Haynes. Bequeathed in 1834 by his sister, Miss Letitia Haynes.’

I knew immediately that I had come across the name somewhere, and soon remembered where. ‘That must be the Archdeacon Haynes who met such an odd end at Barchester. I’ve read his obituary in the Gentleman’s Magazine. May I take the box home? Do you know whether there’s anything interesting in it?’

The librarian was quite willing for me to take the box and examine it at my leisure. ‘I’ve never looked inside it myself,’ he said, ‘though I’ve always meant to. I’m fairly sure it’s the box our old Master once said the college should never have accepted. He told Martin that years ago. He also said that, as long as he controlled the library, it should never be opened. Martin told me about it and said he was terribly eager to know what was inside. But the Master was librarian, and always kept the box in his residence, so no one could get at it during his time. When he died, his heirs took it away by mistake, and it was only returned a few years ago. I can’t think why I haven’t opened it. But since I have to leave Cambridge this afternoon, you had better have the first look. I think I can trust you not to publish anything undesirable in our catalogue.’

I took the box home and examined its contents, then consulted the librarian about publication. He has given me permission to make a story from them, provided I disguise the identities of the people involved, so I will see what I can do.

The material consists mainly, of course, of diaries and letters. Space must determine how much I quote and how much I summarise. To understand the situation properly, I have had to do a little research—not very difficult research. The excellent text and illustrations in the Barchester volume of Bell’s Cathedral Series have made it much easier.

Today, when you enter the choir of Barchester Cathedral, you pass through a screen of metal and coloured marble designed by Sir Gilbert Scott. You find yourself in what I must call a very bare place with detestable furnishings. The stalls are modern and have no canopies. Fortunately, the dignitaries’ places and the names of the endowed cathedral posts have been preserved, and are marked on small brass plates attached to the stalls. The organ is in the upper gallery, and the visible part of its case is Gothic. The screen behind the altar and its surroundings are like all the others.

Careful engravings from a hundred years ago show a very different scene. The organ stands on a massive classical screen. The stalls are also classical and very massive. A wooden canopy stands over the altar, with urns at its corners. Farther east is a solid wooden altar screen, also classical in design. In its pediment is a triangle surrounded by rays, enclosing certain Hebrew letters in gold. Cherubs gaze at them. At the eastern end of the stalls, on the north side, is a pulpit with a large sounding-board above it. The floor is paved in black and white marble. Two ladies and a gentleman admire the overall effect. From other sources, I gather that the archdeacon’s stall, then as now, was beside the bishop’s throne at the south-eastern end of the stalls. His house almost faces the church’s west front: a fine red-brick building from the time of William the Third.

Here, in 1810, Dr Haynes, already a mature man, came to live with his sister. He had long wanted the office, but his predecessor refused to leave until he had reached ninety-two. About a week after he had held a modest celebration of that ninety-second birthday, one morning late in the year, Dr Haynes hurried cheerfully into his breakfast room, rubbing his hands and humming a tune. The sight that greeted him checked his good spirits. His sister sat in her usual place behind the tea urn, but she was bent forward, sobbing uncontrollably into her handkerchief. ‘What—what is the matter? What bad news?’ he began. ‘Oh, Johnny, haven’t you heard? The poor dear archdeacon!’ ‘The archdeacon, yes? What is it—is he ill?’ ‘No, no. They found him on the stairs this morning. It’s so shocking.’ ‘Can it be! Dear, dear, poor Pulteney! Had he suffered some sort of seizure?’ ‘They don’t think so, and that’s almost the worst part. It seems to have been entirely the fault of their stupid maid, Jane.’ Dr Haynes paused. ‘I don’t quite understand, Letitia. How was the maid to blame?’ ‘Well, as far as I can make out, a stair rod was missing, and she never mentioned it. The poor archdeacon put his foot right on the edge of the step—you know how slippery that oak is—and it seems he must have fallen nearly the whole flight and broken his neck. It’s so sad for poor Miss Pulteney. Of course, they’ll dismiss the girl at once. I never liked her.’ Miss Haynes gave way to grief again, though eventually it eased enough for her to eat some breakfast. Not so her brother. After standing silently at the window for several minutes, he left the room and did not appear again that morning.

I need only add that the careless maid was dismissed immediately. Very shortly afterwards, however, the missing stair rod was found beneath the stair carpet—further proof, if any were needed, of her extreme stupidity and carelessness.

For many years, Dr Haynes’s ability, which seems to have been considerable, had marked him out as Archdeacon Pulteney’s likely successor. He was not disappointed. He was duly installed, and began enthusiastically to carry out the duties of his position. Much of his diaries is taken up with exclamations about the confusion in which Archdeacon Pulteney had left the business of his office and its documents. Payments due from Wringham and Barnswood had gone uncollected for something like twelve years, and most could no longer be recovered. No inspection had been held for seven years. Four chancels were almost beyond repair. The people the archdeacon had appointed as deputies had been nearly as incapable as he was. It was almost a cause for gratitude that this state of affairs had not been allowed to continue. A friend’s letter confirms this view. ‘The one who holds things back,’ it says, in a rather cruel reference to the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians, ‘has been removed at last. My poor friend! What a scene of confusion awaits you! I give you my word that the last time I crossed his threshold, he could not lay his hands on a single paper, hear a syllable I said, or remember one fact about my business. But now, thanks to a careless maid and a loose stair carpet, there is some hope that necessary business can be done without completely losing both one’s voice and one’s temper.’ This letter was tucked into a pocket in the cover of one of the diaries.

There can be no doubt about the new archdeacon’s zeal and enthusiasm. ‘Give me only time to bring some appearance of order to the countless errors and complications confronting me, and I shall gladly and sincerely join the aged Israelite in the canticle which too many, I fear, repeat only with their lips.’ I find this reflection in a letter, not a diary. The doctor’s friends seem to have returned his letters to his surviving sister. He did not, however, limit himself to reflections. His enquiries into the rights and duties of his office were thorough and businesslike. In one place, he calculated that three years would just be enough to put the Archdeaconry’s business on a proper footing. The estimate seems to have been exact. For precisely three years, he worked on reforms. But at the end of that time, I look in vain for the promised Nunc dimittis. He had found a new field of activity. Until then, his duties had kept him from attending Cathedral services more than occasionally. Now he began to take an interest in the building and its music. I have no time to dwell on his struggles with the organist, an elderly gentleman who had held his post since 1786. They achieved no notable success. More relevant is his sudden enthusiasm for the Cathedral itself and its furnishings. There is a draft of a letter to Sylvanus Urban, which I do not think was ever sent, describing the choir stalls. As I have said, these were comparatively recent: from about 1700, in fact.

‘The archdeacon’s stall stands at the south-east end, west of the bishop’s throne, now so worthily occupied by the truly excellent prelate who honours the See of Barchester. It is distinguished by some curious ornaments. Besides the coat of arms of Dean West, through whose efforts all the choir’s internal furnishings were completed, the eastern end of the prayer desk has three small but remarkable statuettes in the grotesque style. One is an exquisitely modelled cat. Its crouching posture conveys with admirable spirit the suppleness, watchfulness and cunning of that formidable enemy of the mouse genus. Opposite it is a figure seated on a throne, wearing the symbols of royalty. But the carver has not tried to portray an earthly king. The long robe draped around him carefully conceals his feet. Yet neither his crown nor his cap can hide the pointed ears and curving horns that reveal his origin in Tartarus. The hand resting on his knee is armed with terrifyingly long, sharp claws. Between these two figures stands a shape wrapped in a long cloak. At first glance, it might be mistaken for a monk or “grey-robed friar”: its head is hooded, and a knotted cord hangs from somewhere around its waist. A little examination, however, leads to a very different conclusion. The knotted cord soon proves to be a noose, held by a hand almost hidden within the drapery. The sunken features and, horrible to relate, the torn flesh over the cheekbones proclaim the King of Terrors. These figures clearly come from a skilled chisel. If any of your correspondents can cast light on their origin and meaning, I shall owe a much greater debt to your valuable magazine.’
The paper contains more description, which is of considerable interest now that the woodwork has disappeared. A paragraph at the end is worth quoting:

‘Recent research into the Chapter accounts has shown me that, contrary to frequent reports, the stalls were not carved by Dutch artists. The work was done by a man named Austin, a native of this city or district. The timber came from a nearby oak wood called Holywood, owned by the Dean and Chapter. On a recent visit to the parish in which it stands, I learnt from its elderly and truly respectable clergyman that traditions still survived among the inhabitants about the great size and age of the oaks used to supply the materials for the stately structure described, however imperfectly, above. One tree in particular, near the middle of the grove, was remembered as the Hanging Oak. That name’s appropriateness is confirmed by the quantity of human bones found in the earth around its roots. At certain times of year, too, people who wanted their affairs to succeed, whether in love or in the ordinary business of life, would hang little figures or puppets from its branches. These were crudely made of straw, twigs and similar country materials.’

So much for the archdeacon’s archaeological enquiries. Let us return to his life as we can gather it from his diaries. Throughout the first three years of hard, careful work, they show him in high spirits. During this time, no doubt, he deserved the reputation for hospitality and courtesy mentioned in his obituary. Afterwards, as time passed, I see a shadow coming over him, destined to grow utterly black. I cannot help thinking it must have shown in his outward behaviour. He confided many of his fears and troubles to his diary; he had no other outlet for them. He was unmarried, and his sister was not always with him. But I am much mistaken if he told everything he might have told. Here is a series of extracts:

August 30th, 1816—The days are beginning to shorten more noticeably than ever. Now that the Archdeaconry’s papers are in order, I must find more work for the autumn and winter evenings. It is a great blow that Letitia’s health will not allow her to stay through these months. Why not continue my Defence of Episcopacy? It may be useful.
September 15th—Letitia has left me for Brighton.
October 11th—Candles lit in the choir for the first time at evening prayers. It came as a shock. I find that I positively shrink from the dark season.

November 17th—I was much struck by the nature of the carving on my desk. I am not sure I had ever noticed it carefully before. An accident drew my attention to it. During the Magnificat, I was, I regret to say, almost overcome by sleep. My hand rested on the back of the carved cat, the nearest to me of the three figures at the end of my stall. I did not know this, as I was not looking that way, until I was startled by an apparent softness—a feeling of rather rough, coarse fur—and a sudden movement, as though the creature were turning its head to bite me. I became fully alert in an instant. I suspect I must have let out a muffled exclamation, for I noticed Mr Treasurer turn his head quickly towards me. The impression of that unpleasant feeling was so strong that I found myself rubbing my hand on my surplice. After prayers, this incident led me to examine the figures more carefully than before. For the first time, I realised how skilfully they were carved.

December 6th—I do indeed miss Letitia’s company. The evenings, after I have worked as long as I can on my Defence, are very trying. The house is too large for a lonely man, and visitors of any kind are too rare. On my way to my room, I have the uncomfortable impression that there is company of some sort. The fact is—I may as well put it plainly to myself—that I hear voices. I am well aware that this is a common symptom of the brain beginning to decay. I believe I would be less disturbed than I am if I suspected that was the cause. I do not—not in the slightest. Nor is there anything in my family history to support such an idea. Work, diligent work, and punctual attention to my duties are my best remedy. I have little doubt they will prove effective.

January 1st—I must admit that my trouble is growing. Last night, when I returned from the Deanery after midnight, I lit my candle to go upstairs. I was nearly at the top when something whispered to me, ‘Let me wish you a happy New Year.’ I could not be mistaken. It spoke clearly and with a peculiar emphasis. If I had dropped my candle, as I very nearly did, I tremble to think what the consequences must have been. As it was, I managed to climb the last flight and was quickly in my room with the door locked. Nothing else disturbed me.

January 15th—Last night I had to come downstairs to my workroom for my watch, which I had accidentally left on the table when I went to bed. I think I was at the top of the last flight when I suddenly had the impression of a sharp whisper in my ear: ‘Take care.’ I clutched the banister and naturally looked round at once. Of course, there was nothing. After a moment, I went on—there was no use turning back—but I very nearly fell. A cat, a large one by the feel of it, slipped between my feet. Again, of course, I saw nothing. It may have been the kitchen cat, but I do not think it was.

February 27th—Something curious happened last night, which I would like to forget. Perhaps writing it here will help me see it in its true proportions. I worked in the library from about nine until ten. The hall and stairs seemed unusually full of what I can only call movement without sound. I mean that there seemed to be constant coming and going, yet whenever I stopped writing to listen, or looked into the hall, the stillness remained absolutely unbroken. Nor did I notice anything I could call a noise when I went to my room earlier than usual, at about half past ten. As it happened, I had told John to come to my room for the letter to the bishop, which I wanted delivered at the Palace early in the morning. He was therefore to stay up and fetch it when he heard me go to bed. For the moment I had forgotten this, although I had remembered to carry the letter to my room. But as I was winding my watch, I heard a light tap at the door and a low voice saying, ‘May I come in?’ I most certainly did hear it. Then I remembered, and picked up the letter from my dressing table, saying, ‘Certainly: come in.’ No one answered my summons. It was now, I strongly suspect, that I made a mistake: I opened the door and held out the letter. There was certainly no one in the passage at that moment. But as I stood there, the door at the far end opened and John appeared with a candle. I asked whether he had come to my door earlier, but I am satisfied he had not. I do not like the situation. Still, although my senses were keenly alert and some time passed before I could sleep, I must admit that I noticed nothing else out of the ordinary.

When spring returned and his sister came to stay for several months, Dr Haynes’s entries became more cheerful. Indeed, no sign of depression appears until early September, when he was left alone again. Now there is evidence that he was troubled once more, and more urgently. I will return to that in a moment. First I must digress to include a document which, rightly or wrongly, I believe has some bearing on the story.

Dr Haynes’s account books, kept with his other papers, show quarterly payments of £25 to J. L. beginning soon after his appointment as archdeacon. On its own, this would have told us nothing. But I connect it with a very dirty, badly written letter which, like another I have quoted, was in a pocket in a diary’s cover. No trace of a date or postmark survives, and it was difficult to decipher. It seems to read:
Dear Sir,

I have been expecting to hear from you these last weeks. Since I have not, I must suppose you did not get my letter saying that my husband and I have fallen on hard times this season. Everything seems to go wrong for us on the farm, and we have no idea where to find the rent. Since we are in this sad position, would you have the great [generosity, probably, but the exact spelling is impossible to reproduce] to send forty pounds? Otherwise, steps will have to be taken, which I would not wish. As you were the cause of my losing my place with Dr Pulteney, I think my request is only fair. You know best what I could say if I were forced to it, but I do not wish anything so unpleasant, being someone who always wants everything around me to be pleasant.
Your obedient servant,
Jane Lee.
In fact, at about the time I suppose this letter was written, there is a payment of £40 to J. L.
We return to the diary:

October 22nd—At evening prayers, during the Psalms, I had the same experience I remember from last year. As before, I was resting my hand on one of the carved figures. I usually avoid the cat now. A change came over it, I was going to say. But that seems to give too much importance to what must, after all, result from some physical condition of my own. At any rate, the wood seemed to grow chilly and soft, as though it were made of wet linen. I can identify the moment I noticed it. The choir was singing the words, ‘Set a godless man to rule over him, and let Satan stand at his right hand.’

The whispering in my house was more persistent tonight. I seemed unable to escape it even in my room. I have not noticed that before. A nervous man—which I am not, and hope I am not becoming—would have been very troubled by it, if not frightened. The cat was on the stairs tonight. I think it always sits there. There is no kitchen cat.

November 15th—Again, I must record something I do not understand. My sleep is greatly disturbed. No clear image appeared, but I was haunted by a vivid impression of wet lips whispering into my ear, very rapidly and emphatically, for some time. Afterwards, I suppose I fell asleep. But a feeling that someone had laid a hand on my shoulder woke me with a start. To my intense alarm, I found myself standing at the top of the lowest flight of the first staircase. Moonlight shone brightly enough through the large window for me to see a large cat on the second or third step. I can make no comment. I crept back up to bed; I do not know how. Yes, mine is a heavy burden. [A line or two follows, scratched out. I think I can read something like ‘acted for the best’.]

Not long afterwards, it is clear to me, the archdeacon’s resolve began to weaken under the pressure of these experiences. I omit the cries and prayers that first appeared in December and January and became increasingly frequent. They would be unnecessarily painful and distressing. Throughout this time, however, he stubbornly clung to his post. Why he did not claim ill health and take refuge at Bath or Brighton, I cannot say. My impression is that it would have done him no good. I think he was the sort of man who would have collapsed at once if he admitted defeat by these disturbances—and that he knew it. He did try to ease them by inviting people to stay. He recorded the result as follows:
January 7th—I have persuaded my cousin Allen to spend a few days with me. He is to have the room next to mine.
January 8th—A still night. Allen slept well, but complained of the wind. My own experiences were as before: still whispering and whispering. What is it he wants to say?
January 9th—Allen thinks this is a very noisy house. He also thinks my cat an unusually large and fine specimen, but very wild.

January 10th—Allen and I were in the library until eleven. Twice he left me to see what the maids were doing in the hall. On his second return, he told me he had seen one of them going through the door at the end of the passage. He said that, if his wife were here, she would soon make them behave better. I asked what colour dress the maid wore. He said grey or white. I supposed it would be.
January 11th—Allen left today. I must be firm.

The words ‘I must be firm’ occur again and again in the days that follow. Sometimes they are the only entry. On those occasions, the handwriting is unusually large, and the words are dug so hard into the paper that the pen must have broken.

Apparently, the archdeacon’s friends noticed no change in his behaviour. This gives me a high opinion of his courage and determination. The diary tells us no more about his last days than I have already indicated. The end must be told in the obituary’s polished language:

The morning of February 26th was cold and stormy. At an early hour, the servants had reason to enter the front hall of the home of the much-mourned subject of this account. Imagine their horror when they saw their beloved and respected master lying on the main staircase’s landing in a position that aroused the gravest fears. Help was called. Everyone was deeply shocked to discover that he had suffered a brutal, murderous attack. His spine was broken in more than one place. This might have resulted from a fall: the stair carpet appeared to be loose at one point. But there were also injuries to his eyes, nose and mouth, as though inflicted by some savage animal. Horrible to relate, these had left his features unrecognisable. Needless to say, the spark of life was entirely extinguished. According to respected medical authorities, it had been so for several hours. The person or persons responsible for this mysterious outrage remain equally shrouded in mystery. Even the most energetic speculation has so far failed to suggest an answer to the sorrowful puzzle presented by this appalling event.

The writer goes on to consider the likelihood that the works of Mr Shelley, Lord Byron and Mr Voltaire helped bring about the disaster. He ends by hoping, rather vaguely, that the event may ‘serve as an example to the rising generation’. But this part of his remarks need not be quoted in full.

I had already concluded that Dr Haynes was responsible for Dr Pulteney’s death. But the incident involving the carved figure of death on the archdeacon’s stall was very puzzling. It was easy enough to guess that it had been carved from the Hanging Oak, but proving this seemed impossible. However, I visited Barchester, partly to discover whether anything remained of the woodwork. One of the canons introduced me to the curator of the local museum, who, my friend said, was more likely than anyone else to know something about it. I told him about the description of certain carved figures and coats of arms formerly on the stalls, and asked whether any survived. He showed me Dean West’s coat of arms and some other fragments. These, he said, had come from an old resident who had once also owned a figure—perhaps one of those I was asking about. There was something very odd about that figure, he said. ‘The old man told me he had picked it up in a timber yard, where he also got the pieces that still survive, and taken it home for his children. On his way, he was fiddling with it when it came apart into two pieces in his hands and a piece of paper fell out. He picked that up and, barely noticing that it had writing on it, put it in his pocket and later in a vase on his mantelpiece. Not long ago, I was at his house and happened to pick up the vase. I turned it over to see whether it had any marks, and the paper fell into my hand. When I handed it to him, the old man told me the story I’ve just told you and said I could keep the paper. It was crumpled and rather torn, so I mounted it on a card, which I have here. If you can tell me what it means, I shall be very glad—and, I may add, considerably surprised.’
He handed me the card. The writing on the paper was old-fashioned but quite legible. This is what it said:

When I grew in the wood
I was watered with blood.
Now in the church I stand.
Whoever touches me with his hand,
If his hand is bloody,
I advise him to beware,
Or he may be taken away,
Whether by night or day,
But chiefly when the wind blows high
On a night in February.
This I dreamt, 26 February, in the year 1699. JOHN AUSTIN.
‘I suppose it’s a charm or a spell. Wouldn’t you call it something of that sort?’ said the curator.
‘Yes,’ I said, ‘I suppose one might. What happened to the figure it was hidden in?’
‘Oh, I forgot,’ he said. ‘The old man told me it was so ugly, and frightened his children so much, that he burnt it.’
